one_liner: Small Linux-only C++17 static-file HTTP/1.1 server on raw epoll; ~1.4-1.6x single-worker nginx on 1-8 KB files.
what_it_does: ehttpd is a standalone executable (not a library) that serves files from one document root over plain HTTP/1.1 GET/HEAD, configured only by command-line flags (--port, --root, --workers, --timeout, --max-conns, --address, --stats). It supports keep-alive, pipelining, ETag/If-None-Match 304s and graceful shutdown. It can stand in for nginx only as a bare static origin; there is no config file, TLS, proxying, compression or virtual hosting.
how_it_is_fast: Each worker thread owns its own SO_REUSEPORT listener and edge-triggered epoll loop, so connections never cross threads and there are no locks (shared-nothing reactor-per-core). Bodies of 8 KB or less are pread into the response buffer and sent with the header in one send() call, which the author's threshold sweep measured at +44% at 1 KB and +26% at 8 KB over always using sendfile; larger bodies use sendfile(2). A per-worker open-file-descriptor cache (fstat revalidation on a 2 s TTL) removes open/fstat/close from hot requests, and a resumable byte-at-a-time parser records offsets and returns string_views, so parsing does no heap allocation.
when_to_use: Serving a small set of hot, small (roughly 1-8 KB) static files over plain HTTP/1.1 on Linux, where per-request CPU cost is what limits you
Behind a TLS-terminating load balancer or CDN, as a minimal static origin that needs only GET/HEAD, keep-alive and ETag revalidation
Memory-constrained boxes or sidecars: the author measured 4.1-5.2 MB RSS under load vs 10.4-10.5 MB for single-worker nginx
As a readable reference for a reactor-per-core epoll/SO_REUSEPORT/sendfile server: about 1,700 lines of C++ plus about 820 lines of tests, with design notes, and CI runs ASan and TSan jobs
when_not_to_use: Payloads of 64 KB and up: the author measured parity with nginx (0.94x-1.02x), so there is nothing to gain

Anything beyond bare static files: no TLS, HTTP/2, request bodies (non-zero Content-Length gives 413, Transfer-Encoding gives 501), proxying, CGI, gzip, virtual hosts, access logs, IPv6 or non-Linux platforms
Media or download serving: no Range requests (per the source) and only 14 file extensions get a MIME type; .mp4, .pdf, .xml, .woff and others go out as application/octet-stream

Document roots larger than the page cache: open(), pread() and sendfile() run on the event-loop thread, so a cold disk read stalls every connection on that worker, and SO_REUSEPORT gives no work stealing
Production use that needs a track record: 0 stars, no releases or tags, no issues filed, and all 13 commits were pushed together on 2026-08-08

integration.dependencies: none beyond libc and pthreads; CMake 3.16+ to build; wrk and nginx only for the benchmark script
integration.min_toolchain: C++17, CMake 3.16; CI builds with the gcc and clang on GitHub's ubuntu-latest image (versions not pinned)
integration.platforms: Linux only (epoll, sendfile, timerfd, eventfd, accept4, SO_REUSEPORT); IPv4 only
integration.thread_safety: Shared-nothing: each worker thread owns its listener, connections, file cache and timer wheel, with no locks; README reports a clean ThreadSanitizer run and CI runs a TSan job
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it replaces an nginx 'root + sendfile + keep-alive' static location only; nothing in an nginx config carries over, and TLS, Range, gzip, logging, proxying and virtual hosts are all missing

gotchas: The file cache revalidates by fstat() on the descriptor it already holds, so a file replaced by rename (atomic deploys) or deleted keeps being served from the old inode until eviction or restart; only in-place edits that change mtime (second granularity) or size are picked up

Every worker binds with SO_REUSEPORT, so starting a second ehttpd on a port already in use does not fail; the kernel silently splits connections between the two processes (the author's integration test works around exactly this)

The listening socket is registered level-triggered and accept_batch() just returns on EMFILE/ENFILE, so running out of file descriptors likely makes the worker spin in epoll_wait at full CPU until descriptors free up (read from the code, not tested)

HTTP semantics are minimal: If-None-Match must equal the ETag string exactly (no list, W/ or *), If-Modified-Since is ignored although Last-Modified is sent, responses carry no Date or Cache-Control header, a directory path without a trailing slash returns 403 instead of a redirect, and keep-alive connections close after 10,000 requests
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over uhttp when you cannot rely on io_uring: uhttp needs liburing 2.5+ and C++20, while ehttpd needs only epoll and C++17; uhttp's benchmark is stronger, though (wrk on 6 cores, 3 interleaved runs, byte-matched headers, +40-54% vs tuned nginx). Pick H2O instead whenever you need a real server (HTTP/2, experimental HTTP/3, library mode); the framework siblings (Drogon, Crow, Lwan, Sogou Workflow) serve dynamic handlers, which ehttpd does not have at all.
verified_claims_summary: The author's bench/run.sh ran one ehttpd worker against one nginx worker (version not stated; sendfile, keep-alive and open-file cache on, logging and gzip off) on a 2-core Intel Xeon @ 2.10 GHz under Linux 6.18, with a single wrk thread at 50 connections for 10 s over loopback, and got 152,931 vs 96,792 req/s on 1 KB (1.58x; 1.51x-1.67x over four runs), 1.39x on 8 KB, 0.94x on 64 KB and under half nginx's RSS, built with -O2 -DNDEBUG on an unnamed compiler. The numbers are first-party, response headers were not equalized (ehttpd sends no Date header), and both of ehttpd's small-file rows sit near 151-153k req/s, which may mean the single wrk thread was close to its own limit.
status_note: MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor, but all 13 commits landed in one push on 2026-08-08 (one passing CI run), with no releases, issues, later commits or Hacker News mentions, so 'active' is unproven.
